titleStmt.title: Towards Model-Checking Security of Real-Time Java Software

analytic.title: Towards Model-Checking Security of Real-Time Java Software

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: More and more software libraries and applications in high-performance computing and distributed systems are coded using the Java programming language. The correctness of such pieces of code w.r.t. a given set of security policies often depends on the correct handling of timing between concurrent or recurrent events.

Model-checking has proven to be an effective tool for verifying the correctness of software. In spite of the growing importance of this application area of formal methods, though, no approach exists that targets the problem of verifying the correctness of real-time software w.r.t. timed specifications. The few existing works focus on very different problems, such as schedulability analysis of Java tasks. In this paper we present an approach combining rule-based static analysis together with symbolic execution of Java code to extract networks of timed automata from existing software and then use Uppaal to model-check them against timed specifications. We show through a real-world case study that this approach can be helpful in model-checking security policies of real-time Java software.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: High-Performance Computing (HPC), Internet of Things (IoT), Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs), Automotive Systems are examples of recent and growing areas where real-time software plays a key role. Many of them are intrinsically safety and security critical. While safety critical systems have requirements expressible in the form of invariants that are expected to hold for the entire system life, security critical systems are characterized by requirements that fall into the well known Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA) triad. It is thus becoming crucial to have appropriate techniques and tools that guide the engineer through the task of formally verifying existing software. We underline that most of the existing approaches in literature focus on certifying that protocols or high level software models are safe and secure, but this does not imply that actual implementations of those protocols and models are exempted from bugs. For instance, in recent years two popular bugs, Heartbleed 1 and GOTOfail 2 , affected popular implementations of the SSL protocol, putting several production environments and service providers at risk. 1 https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2014-0160 2 https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2014-1266 Software model-checking techniques can be employed in order to certify the correctness of actual pieces of code w.r.t. given specifications, while alternative approaches such as systematic testing can only conjecture it [1]. The specifications used in software model-checking can, in principle, be used to express the safety and security requirements to be checked (e.g. [2]). A prerequisite to apply software model-checking, though, is to have a finite-state model of the software under investigation that is as faithful as possible in describing the behavior of the original piece of code, at least w.r.t. the checked specifications. The two main research questions that drive our work are: (i) how to extract a finite-state representation of real-time Java code, and (ii) how faithful is such a representation when checking safety and security policies of software.

We present a model-checking methodology for Java software, together with a prototype implementation. The choice of Java is motivated by the fact that it is a popular choice both in high performance computing and real-time software [3], [4]. The core components of the methodology employ rule-based approaches in order to: compute the finite-state representation of each Java thread and detect the time constraints between events encoded in the Java program. With a case study, we show how to use the tool to discover a real bug that was present in a real-world project.

div.head: II. OVERVIEW
div.p: We present a methodology for extracting a network of timed automata from Java code. The overall task can be seen as the combination of several static analyses sub-tasks. A graphical representation of our methodology is given in Fig. 1.

The parsing step consists in extracting an intermediate representation of the entire Java project. We exploit the Eclipse JDT parser for Java 8 to produce a reduced abstract syntax tree (AST) from the code, and we store it into a nosql database for saving time when the methodology is used interactively by the user.

A successive phase traverses the AST and along the way it annotates timestamp variables. Inspired by [5], and using a list of common Java methods manipulating timestamps as well as Java types used to represent time values, we label as timestamp variables those variables in the program that are used as timestamps along the Fig. 1: Our methodology at a glance program (e.g. because they are used to store the result of method java.lang.System.currentTimeMillis, or because they are passed as input to the java.lang.Thread.sleep method). We expect that the list of Java methods and types used to identify timestamps in a program can be maintained in a centralized way, together with the implementation of the methodology itself, and that the user is in principle allowed to add custom types and methods and extend such list. Ideally, finer implementations of the methodology can allow communities of users to share their customizations, and the knowledge acquired along the analysis of Java real-time software.

The next step focuses on extracting discrete states and transitions representing the program discrete behavior. To this aim, we ask the user to provide a set of first-order predicates over a subset of the program variables. Through them, it is possible to abstract each concrete configuration of the program variables onto a single first-order predicate. If one or more variables have no associated predicate, then we assume they can assume any value. The predicates specified by the user can relate at any time the concrete states of k variables. Successively, each instruction ι of the program is interpreted as a first-order predicate α(ι)(s, t), relating the abstract state of variables before executing the given instruction (s), to the abstract state of the same variables after executing it (t). Notice that it is in general not possible to give a firstorder interpretation of any arbitrary Java instruction 3 . For this reason, this step employs a set of rules that can be extended over time in order to detect relevant patterns appearing in Java programs. In case that none of the rules applies to the Java instruction under analysis, we map the instruction onto the tautology binary predicate α(ι) = , relating any source configuration to any target configuration. This ensures that every abstract transition α(ι) is an existential abstraction of the concrete instruction ι, for any ι. To check that there can 3 think for example to the invocation of a recursive method on some arbitrary input exist a transition α(ι) from s to t we use Z3, a state-of-the-art SMT solver [6].

The successive phase extracts timing information encoded in the program. This is achieved identifying a suitable set of clock variables tracking the time relations between events as they are handled by the program. Since the final model will be a network of timed automata, this consists in inferring:
• which clock variables should be in the timed automata,
• which clock constraints enable the discrete transitions of each timed automaton, and • what discrete transitions should reset the clock variables.

At the moment, this stage takes advantage of the timestamp annotations added in the previous stage, together with additional clock annotations added by the user. A statespace optimization step concludes the methodology, where sequences of transitions that do not branch and differ only for the value of the program-counter are collapsed in a single transition. Even this simple idea proves to be very helpful in reducing the size of the extracted timed automata. This reduction can be applied whenever the specification does not look at the value of the program-counter.
The network of timed automata resulting from applying our methodology can be used for several purposes, e.g.:

• for model-checking safety and security policies against some logical property provided by the user (e.g. using Uppaal); • for simulation purposes (e.g. using Uppaal); and • as a documentation means, giving a high-level view of the code (e.g. for software (re-)engineering purposes).

In this work, we stress the fact that the model-checking purpose is helpful in proving that pieces of real-time Java software are indeed safe and secure. Using the formalization of security properties by Clarkson and Schneider [7], we claim that our approach can be applied to model-check a sub-class of hyper-properties specifications, e.g. k-safety or kliveness hyperproperties, i.e. safety or liveness specifications that can be falsified by systematically exploring up to k execution traces of the program under investigation.
For this work we restrict the methodology to model-check a fixed number of threads, thus ignoring the instructions that lead to creation of new threads.

We also underline that the methodology is designed to be interactive: if the user finds the returned network of timed automata not precise enough for checking the desired security policy, he or she can provide different abstraction predicates and generate a more refined discrete component, or alternatively add more detailed clock information about the time handling of events by the program itself.

Since the parsing phase is rather standard, and techniques for labeling the timed variables have been extensively described in [5], in this work we will describe how to extract the discrete and the timing component from the Java source code.

div.head: A. Intruder model
div.p: An intruder (or attacker) model is necessary when the security of a system is checked. Working with security protocols, the most popular intruder model is probably the Dolev-Yao attacker [8]. The key idea behind it is that all participants are expected to follow their role in the protocol under investigation, while the intruder is freely allowed to send messages in any order and with any content, store messages for later use and forge new messages. The intruder, though, is not allowed to decrypt an encrypted message payload without the proper (symmetric or asymmetric) key. At a very abstract level, we can see the attacker as a hostile environment playing against the protocol participants from the outside.

In this sense, we assume an intruder model that is very similar to the Dolev-Yao one. We replace the protocol with the code of the threads under analysis, the participating actors with the chosen Java threads, and the hostile environment with the possible configurations assumed by the variables affecting the behavior of the threads under investigation.

Our intruder model for software is general and can simulate an active attacker that chooses a strategy to play against the threads. To understand the motivations behind our intruder model, let us first remind that sanitizing the user inputs is a mandatory step when writing production software. On the other side, it is also very common that programmers forget to sanitize some of the input parameters, or the sanitation procedure is incomplete. This leads to vulnerabilities in the code that may remain silent in production systems for years, before being noticed. In the meantime, a smart hacker can discover them either by accident or by carefully analyzing how the application reacts to his/her stimuli. Such vulnerabilities may allow to invoke pieces of code after having assigned arbitrary values to variables that affect their behavior, i.e. forging a hostile environment around the code. This explains the key intuition behind our intruder model.

div.head: IV. ABSTRACTING THE TIMING OF EVENTS
div.p: The time model for extracting timed automata from Java code can be summarized with the following rules:
• reading the system clock can take any time;

• the invocation of java.lang.Thread.sleep(t) holds the thread in the same state for t time units; • the other Java instructions take zero time to be executed. This is motivated by the fact that Java programs can update (all or some of) its timestamps only after having read the current system clock. Until then, all the time-dependent actions encoded in the program may only refer to the previous values of the timestamps. It can be proven that a similarity relation exists between standard Java executions and Java executions with our time model. On the other side, it is possible that a real-time specification does not hold if we don't assume that the Java code waits for a bounded amount of time between any two system clock reads. For this reason, if needed, our methodology allows the user to specify a maximum amount of time to wait when reading the system clock.

Let us underline that for this work we assume a fair realtime scheduler for the checked Java treads, i.e. we rule out the possibility that a thread may starve due to a bad scheduling (at the level of the JVM or of the operating system).

Let us now recall the basic notions about timed automata. A timed automaton is a state transition system P = (S, S 0 , T, C, I, G, R) such that (S, S 0 , T ) is a finitestate automaton, C is a finite set of clocks and Γ is the set of boolean combinations of predicates of the form c ∼ c or c ∼ k, where c and c are clock variables, k is a natural number, and ∼∈ {<, =, >} is a comparison operator. I : S → Γ maps each discrete state to its time invariant, G : T → Γ maps each discrete transition to one (possibly universal) enabling clock guard, and R : T → 2 C maps each discrete transition to zero or more clock variables to reset when taking the transition.

Let us underline the Java language do not allow to represent directly clock variables as intended by timed automata. They keep track of time passage by means of timestamps, and along the program the latter are compared against the system clock. We assume that each thread associates a clock variable c(t 1 , t 2 ) ∈ C to each pair of timestamp variables (t 1 , t 2 ) found by the "Annotate Timestamps" stage (cfr. Fig 1). If the user manually specifies additional timestamp variables, more clock variables will be generated. Intuitively, every clock variable c(t 1 , t 2 ) is used to keep track of the difference between the timestamps. Thus, every clock condition of the form c(t 1 , t 2 ) ∼ k holds iff t 1t 2 ∼ k, for any comparison operator ∼∈ {<, ≤, =} and constant k ∈ N.
At the moment we classify timestamp variables as follows:
• now-timestamp: these are the timestamp variables that are updated only for storing the value of the system clock,

• constant-timestamp: these are the timestamps that are assigned only once along the life of a thread. We then restrict our analysis to time constraints that can be expressed using such timestamps in the program. First of all, we associate a clock variable c(t 1 , t 2 ) to the timestamps t 1 and t 2 only if t 1 is a now-timestamp and t 2 is a constanttimestamp, thus reducing the number of clock variables in the network of timed automata. This equals to assigning a clock variable c(t 1 ) that only depends on the now-timestamp t 1 , and make t 2 a parameter of the timed automaton appearing in the clock expressions. Indeed, for any constant k ∈ N,
div.formula: c(t 1 , t 2 ) ∼ k iff t 1 -t 2 ∼ k (by definition) iff c(t 1 ) ∼ t 2 + k,
div.p: and by our assumption the expression t 2 +k ∈ N is constant as well. As a consequence, each time the expression t 1 ∼ t 2 + k guarding some code block appears in the source code, we add the clock constraint c(t 1 ) ∼ t 2 + k to enter the abstraction of the code block, and its negation to skip it.

From the point of view of security analysis, notice that marking t 2 as a parameter of the timed automaton means to give one more chance to the intruder to create a hostile environment where the piece of code could be executed. This in turn implies that we need to model-check all the possible (abstract) values that parameter t 2 may assume.

Note that updating a timestamp in the Java code does not change the discrete component of the automaton. On the other side, our methodology must understand when a clock variable c(t 1 , t 2 ) should be reset. Under our assumptions, since the only timestamp to be updated is t 1 and it is used for checking the current real time, it is enough to reset the clock c(t 1 ) when t 1 reads the system clock for the first time, while successive reads of the system clock can just be ignored.

If we want to check a specification under the assumption that the Java threads wait a limited amount of time before reading the system clock, the tool allows to add a dedicated clock variable c prog, while the invariant c prog < T P ROG is assigned to the locations where the system clock is read. The parameter T P ROG is not modifiable by the intruder.

div.head: V. CASE STUDY
div.p: We have implemented our methodology in a prototype tool. In the tool the user specifies the program he/she wants to abstract and a set of predicates over the program variables. The method in Fig. 4 constitutes the body of a Java thread that is part of a project named Apache Kafka4 , a popular distributed streaming platform allowing to implement a publish-subscribe service to streams of data.

The considered piece of code implements a poll mechanism, where a server is periodically checked for being ready, and if not, it is enforced to become ready. That method contained a bug5 appearing when the parameter timeout assumes a negative value, or a big enough value, such that expression now + timeout overflows and becomes smaller than now. The bug was found "out of the box", by the programmers' own admission, and we claim that our methodology could have helped in finding it.

In our case study, the thread security requirement is an availability requirement: whenever the thread exits, the server must be in its ready state, denoting that the service is available to the other threads in the system.

To this aim, the user instructs the tool to use two abstract variables, is_ready and coordinator_known. Then the user specifies the following first-order interpretation of method ensureCoordinatorReady(): (assert (= is_ready_1 true)), while method coordinatorUnknown is abstracted as follows:

(assert (= __return__ coordinator_known)), where __return__ is an auxiliary SMT variable used to store the result the method invocation. All other methods are abstracted with a first-order tautology, meaning that they have no effect on the variables is_ready and coordinator_known. Finally, the user specifies that he/she wants to verify a system with only the poll thread. The tool automatically recognizes two timestamps, viz. deadline and now, the former being a constant-timestamp and the latter being a now-timestamp.

Fig. 5 reports a graphical representation of the timed automaton extracted from the thread poll. Note that the actual state space of the discrete component is given by 204 states, i.e. 4 configurations of the two boolean variables is_ready and coordinator_ready, times the 17 values of the program-counter register, times the 3 possible abstract values of parameter deadline: deadline < 0, deadline = 0, and deadline > 0. In the figure we only make explicit the value of the program-counter register, for the sake of readability. The timed automaton contains one clock variable now, and one parameter deadline. The security requirement can be encoded with the following TCTL formula: AF (is_ready = true). Uppaal takes less than a second to find the following counter example path: (σ, pc = @0) → (σ, pc = @1) → (σ, pc = @2) → (σ, pc = @3), where σ = deadline < 0 ∧ is ready = false ∧ coordinator known = true, and a simple code inspection allows to understand that the found counterexample is not spurious, i.e. is not added by the abstraction process, but it can happen with concrete executions of the method.

div.head: VI. RELATED WORK
div.p: In spite of the extensive use of Java in both highperformance computing and real-time software, only few authors (e.g. see [9], [5], [10]) focused on timed automata extraction from source code written in a general purpose programming language, as well as model-checking code implementing real-time distributed algorithms. Some of them focus on the extraction of control flow automata [9], [5], not taking into account the role played by program variables along the execution, and not allowing to check specifications that look at the state of the program variables. Others focus on schedulability analysis and best-or worst-case execution time [10], [11], but do not consider the correctness w.r.t. timed specifications. To the best of our knowledge, none of them considers the problem of model-checking correctness, safety and security requirements of Java code. This paper is a first step towards filling the gap.

Herber et al. [9] model-check SystemC programs, extracting timed automata from them. They also assume that most of the instructions have a zero-time model. Our approach, in contrast to theirs, can handle programs with operations on variables of non-integer types and we extract clock variables from timestamps.

Blast [12] is a software model-checker for C programs. Blast has several limitations that our approach overcomes: they do not handle timing of events nor real-time specifications; they extract control flow automata from C functions; they can only check reachability of program locations; they only deal with integer and boolean program variables. Java Path Finder [13] and Bandera [14] are popular modelcheckers for Java programs. The former uses a Java Virtual Machine that explores symbolic paths of the Java bytecode under analysis. The latter employs program slicing techniques for abstracting program variables that do not affect the verified specification. While this is good for model-checking, it does not allow to extract a finite-state model for software (re-)engineering purposes. Both extract untimed models from Java code, and allow to check only untimed specifications.

Sen and Mall [15] apply several static analysis tools for reverse engineering a finite-state model from Java bytecode, mostly for documentation purposes. The major difference w.r.t. our approach is that they do not handle time neither in the model nor in the specification, and that they compute a transition system for each object in the program. It means they compute the state-space of each class, based on the abstract states of the latter's private attributes, and compute how a method invocation can move the object from one abstract state to another. The finite-state model of the program is obtained as the combination of the transition systems of the objects used in the program itself. We are interested in employing this technique for abstracting objects used by threads, but we claim that it is not good enough to describe the sequence of intermediate steps taken by a thread (e.g. we may need to know in which order a thread acquires its resources in order to detect a deadlock situation).

In a previous work [16] we employ symbolic path exploration in order to detect bugs stemming from bad operations on timestamps (e.g. passing negative timestamps or allowing overflows/underflows when adding/subtracting timestamps). Since that technique was more focused on finding bugs, it computes an under-approximation of the code and explores it for a finite set of patterns that would reveal a possible bug. In this work, on the other side, we build an over-approximation in the form of a network of timed automata, such that it can be used to check that one or more specifications are satisfied.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: This paper presents a methodology aiming at modelchecking some safety and security requirements against pieces of Java code. The methodology can extract a network of timed automata from the Java code under analysis, and through an interactive workflow, can accept information from the user that drives the process of generating an existential abstraction of the checked code. The process of extracting a model from Java code is cumbersome and error-prone, thus we claim that our methodology can be helpful if plugged into the usual software engineering and re-engineering processes, to prove that a piece of source code fulfills a set of safety and security specifications, provided that the latter can be expressed using the temporal logic TCTL. The presented methodology has been implemented in a prototype tool.

Our work is original in several aspects: first, similar works extracting timed automata from code deal with control flow abstraction [16], [5], [9] and largely overapproximate the visited program states, which in turn means the modelchecking phase is not successful because of the large number of spurious counter-examples introduced. Allowing the user to decide which variable configurations to track, he/she is in control to find the best trade-off between model refinement and feasibility of model-checking. Second, existing approaches for model-checking real-time Java code only focus on the analysis of best-/worst-case execution times, not considering the problem of checking the safety or security of the software. We aim at filling this gap.

It is our goal to extend our approach in several directions. First, we aim at testing the approach with more real-world case studies, handling more complex scenarios with several synchronizing threads, and observe how it scales. Next, techniques for abstracting clocks from source code are needed, since existing ones do not apply to this context [17], [18]. One more line of research is inferring a first set of relevant abstraction predicates automatically from the Java source code under analysis. Ideally, if certain conditions appear as guards of the branching instructions in the code, they may be good candidates to compute a first, automatic, abstract state space of the code under analysis. This kind of heuristic may ease the burden on the user when model-checking the code, not preventing him/her from adding additional information, in case it is needed for completing the verification task. Finally, we intend to integrate existing approaches for worst-case execution time analysis of Java code, in order to model check more complex safety and security specifications that involve real-time in the specification.
